20978-a-hungarian-nabob:
Too many episodes crowd A Hungarian Nabob, its translator owns with a frank plea. She begs Mor Jokai's pardon, keen the tale should charm at first sight. The English text of 1899 trims the growth for new readers' sake.

Jokai's nabob, a rich Hungarian of vast lands and wilder whims, stars here. Old Hungary's feasts, duels, pride, and reforms swirl around his house. Jokai poured his nation's life into huge, warm novels of this kind. This one, his most famed abroad, shows why Hungary crowned him its national storyteller in his own lifetime.
21005-shorty-mccabe-on-the-job:
Do things just happen, or is there a scheme on file somewhere, Shorty McCabe asks. Sewell Ford's 1913 tales put that brash query in Shorty's own slangy mouth. White hopes, trunk murders, and fire heroes crowd his comic roll of the age.

Shorty, a stocky ex-boxer turned gym keeper, meets New York life head-on here. Ford writes in a fast, funny vernacular that won vast fans in his day. Crooks, swells, and soft hearts cross Shorty's mats in quick tales. The book is pure period fun, with a shrewd, kind core beneath its wise-cracking New York surface.
brother-jacob: George Eliot's 1864 novella about a confectioner, his foolish brother Jacob, and a stolen guinea. A small, perfect comedy of provincial life. Eliot's lightest touch, and a gem. Eliot's comedy is as precise as her tragedy is profound.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob: A 1913 entry on Jacob — the supplanting patriarch. Francis Gigot unfolds his scriptural tale. He wrestled the nightly angel. The tribes sprang from the twelve sons. The Israel of the covenant's promise. His Genesis tale is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-job: A 1913 entry on Job — the patient sufferer. Joseph Hontheim unfolds the sacred drama. He blessed the chastening hand. The friends weighed the seemly cause. The whirlwind crowned the holy book. His Uz patience is famed. His 1907 study is famed. His Uz friends are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mesrob: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Mesrob — the Armenian alphabet's maker. Arthur Adolphe Vaschalde honors his famous letters. His pen gave the nation script. Armenia bless the holy name. The fifth century knew his toil. His 439 death is famed. His alphabet is famed.
doe-osti-2571779-cryogenic-optical-and-s: A cryogenic quantum-defect scanner got its DOE station, and this text covers the high-throughput probe. The pages detail the instrument. The quantum materials folks get their tool. The station was cryogenic. The throughput was high. The defects were quantum.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CohenJacob_Cohe:
Jacob Cohen, a historian, wrote for The Nation an article titled 'The Vital Documents,' on the Kennedy assassination's documentary record. This letter, dated July 3, 1966, was written to Cohen about that article.

The Nation's pages were a battleground of the first assassination debate, where critics and defenders of the Warren Commission traded charges about which documents mattered and what they proved. A letter like this one is the debate at ground level: one reader, one article, and the argument joined by mail. The letter is preserved as part of the correspondence the controversy generated.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GibbonsBob_Gibb: A letter from Bob Gibbons to a man named Gary, whose surname is illegible, concerns the Zapruder film, the home movie of the Kennedy assassination. The date attached to the letter in the record reads May 12, 1960, which cannot be right for a film shot in 1963 and is best treated as a garbled date. The letter survives as a researcher's note about the famous film.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VernonBob_Verno: Michael Hytha wrote about Bob Vernon, a lone television maker from Antioch, and an Illinois inmate who claimed Vernon's support. Vernon had come to believe in evidence that challenged the official account of the Kennedy assassination. The article follows a small, stubborn corner of assassination research, far from Washington and the big publishers. It shows how belief in the case spread through local media figures.
tanakh-jps-1917-job:
Job is a wisdom book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation of the Holy Scriptures. It opens in the land of Uz with a man named Job, praised as whole-hearted, upright, and one who shunned evil.

Job holds vast wealth, with seven sons, three daughters, and herds that make him the greatest man of the east. He offers gifts for his children after each feast, lest they have sinned in their hearts. Then the sons of God come before the Lord, and Satan comes among them. Readers enter the Bible's deep test of why the just suffer, told in prose frames and long, fierce verse debate.
the-farmer-boy-the-story-of-jacob:
J. H. Willard retold the Bible story of Jacob for young readers in The Farmer Boy, part of Altemus' Children of the Bible series, printed at Philadelphia in 1905. Jacob stands in a line of boy heroes from Isaac to the boy Jesus.

The tale opens with Abraham, head of the Hebrew tribe, moving with flocks, herds, camels, and servants from place to place. From that stock comes Jacob, the farmer boy of the title. Willard keeps the speech plain and the scenes short, so a child can follow the births, blessings, and tricks that shape the father of a nation.
the-nabob:
Alphonse Daudet's novel The Nabob, translated by W. Blaydes, opens with a long critical introduction rather than the story. Daudet once remarked, the introducer writes, that England was the last foreign country to welcome his novels, which surprised him, since home life mattered greatly to him and to the typical Englishman. In time he won English and American hearts more completely than any contemporary French novelist.

Admirers is too cold a word, the essay argues; friends is heartier and fits better. Some readers found in Daudet a French Dickens, others a refined Mark Twain with a flavour of Cervantes. Most simply enjoyed him, the introducer says, because his writing was steeped in his own charming personality, as a Corot picture is steeped in sunlight.
the-world-english-bible-web-job:
Job appears as book eighteen in the World English Bible, set in the land of Uz. Its hero is blameless, upright, and God-fearing. He turns away from evil, readers are told at once. Seven sons and three daughters fill his house. His wealth includes thousands of sheep and camels. He is called the greatest man in the east.

His sons feast in rotation on their birthdays. Their sisters join the celebrations. After each round Job offers burnt sacrifices for them. He worries they may have cursed God in their hearts. That careful piety makes his coming losses harder. The book then asks why the righteous suffer at all.
